strengths: The paper presents an original and intuitively motivated alternative to pixel- and voxel-aligned Gaussian prediction: differentiable, sub-pixel primitive placement using patch-level heatmaps and soft-argmax, combined with adaptive density and learned multi-view confidence.

The method is technically coherent and end-to-end differentiable, integrating primitive localization, depth-based unprojection, Gaussian parameter decoding, multi-view aggregation, rendering supervision, and geometry regularization into a pose-free pipeline.

Results are strong against the closest baseline, AnySplat. On DL3DV, the method generally improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS while using roughly 3–7 times fewer Gaussians, and the qualitative examples show sharper details and cleaner extrapolated geometry.

The ablation study supports the usefulness of adaptive density and confidence-based aggregation. The pixel-aligned comparisons also show that simply increasing the number of grid-aligned primitives from about 67k to 268k does not improve quality, supporting the broader motivation that placement matters more than primitive count.

The camera-pose results are promising: fine-tuning improves AUC@15 and AUC@30 over pretrained VGGT for every evaluated view count, whereas AnySplat degrades pose estimation. The manuscript is generally clear, and the architecture and qualitative behavior are well illustrated.
weaknesses: Material: The empirical breadth is insufficient for the strong state-of-the-art claim. Only two datasets and three comparison pipelines are evaluated, while several cited pose-free feed-forward methods—including PF3Splat, NoPoSplat, SPFSplat, and VicaSplat—are omitted without a clear explanation. On Charge, the proposed method is not generally best: DepthSplat leads PSNR/SSIM in the 3-, 6-, and 9-view settings, and AnySplat often has better LPIPS.

Material: The experiments do not isolate the central claim that continuous off-grid positioning itself causes the improvement. The detection decoder differs structurally from the pixel baseline and is coupled to adaptive density and confidence. A decisive ablation snapping the learned coordinates to pixel centers, or comparing continuous and grid-constrained locations at identical primitive counts and otherwise identical architecture, is absent.

Material: Efficiency is inferred almost entirely from the number of Gaussians. The paper reports no end-to-end latency, decoder cost, peak memory, model size, or rendering FPS, despite repeatedly claiming faster or more efficient reconstruction. The large VGGT-1B backbone and customized rasterizer make primitive count alone inadequate evidence of practical efficiency.

Material: The claim that rendering supervision improves the backbone's “geometry” is overstated. Camera-pose accuracy improves, but depth is consistently worse than pretrained VGGT on Charge for most metrics and view counts; focal-length improvements are dataset-dependent. No quantitative surface or point-cloud geometry evaluation is provided.

Material: Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript does not specify the sizes or exact identities of the training subsets, optimizer, learning rates, schedule, number of iterations, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, or many sampling details. Training also requires a single GPU with 140 GB of memory, limiting accessibility, and no evidence is provided that the released description is sufficient to reproduce the results.

There are two concrete technical inconsistencies. The stated patch allocation assigns 55% low-, 35% medium-, and 15% high-density patches, totaling 105%—the reported primitive count suggests that 50/35/15 may have been intended. More seriously, the opacity regularizer is written as sum sin(alpha*c); over alpha*c in [0,1], this is minimized at zero and does not encourage values toward both zero and one as claimed unless a missing factor such as pi is intended.

The “self-supervised” framing needs qualification: the decoder fine-tuning requires a pretrained VGGT backbone and explicit teacher losses to VGGT's geometry, where VGGT was trained with geometric supervision. The adaptation uses no new annotations, but the presented evidence does not establish that a 3D foundation model can be trained without labels, as suggested in the conclusion.

The target-view evaluation protocol runs a second backbone pass on the context and target images to obtain target poses. Although this follows AnySplat and does not insert target Gaussians into the reconstructed model, it exposes target-image content during evaluation and differs from standard NVS with known target cameras. Results under ground-truth-pose alignment, together with pose-estimation results reported separately, would make the rendering comparison easier to interpret.

strengths: The central idea—replacing pixel/voxel-aligned Gaussian centers with differentiable, sub-pixel primitive placement—is relevant and technically plausible. It addresses a real inefficiency in feed-forward 3DGS rather than merely modifying the backbone.
The method combines soft-argmax localization, entropy-based density allocation, and confidence-based multi-view fusion in a coherent end-to-end system built on VGGT.

The ablation on DL3DV provides useful evidence: the complete detector reaches 19.09 PSNR, 0.5998 SSIM, and 0.3379 LPIPS with about 38.4K Gaussians per image, outperforming both reported pixel-aligned variants, including one using about 268K Gaussians.

The reported primitive-count reduction is substantial. Across the main comparison, the method uses roughly one-third to one-fifth as many Gaussians as the evaluated alternatives while remaining competitive in rendering quality.
The paper is generally readable, and the diagrams and qualitative comparisons communicate the proposed architecture and intended benefits clearly.
weaknesses: The novel-view evaluation has a consequential protocol problem: target images are included in a second VGGT forward pass to recover target camera poses. Thus evaluation requires access to the very target images being reconstructed, does not demonstrate rendering at a genuinely user-specified unseen camera, and can couple scores to target-image-dependent pose estimation. Different alignment procedures are also used across methods—no correction for the proposed method, scale correction for AnySplat, and optimization for FLARE—so Table 1 does not cleanly isolate representation quality.

The claimed state-of-the-art superiority is overstated. On Charge, the proposed method wins only 3 of 12 reported quality comparisons: VGGT+DepthSplat is substantially better in PSNR and SSIM for the 3-, 6-, and 9-view settings, while AnySplat has better LPIPS for 6, 9, and 25 views. Even on DL3DV, several LPIPS differences are negligible or unfavorable.

The claim that rendering supervision improves the backbone's geometry is not adequately supported. Table 2 shows improved camera-pose AUC but worse depth metrics than the original VGGT in every setting. On Charge, focal-length angular error and the fraction below 3 degrees also become worse. The conclusion nevertheless broadly claims enhanced geometry.

Important mathematical and specification inconsistencies undermine technical clarity. The density proportions are stated as 55%, 35%, and 15%, which sum to 105%. Equation 1 indexes spatial heatmap coordinates using P even though P is defined as the number of primitives/channels. Most seriously, the stated regularizer sum sin(alpha*c), with alpha*c in [0,1], is minimized at zero and therefore does not regularize opacity toward both 0 and 1 as claimed; a missing factor or different formulation appears necessary.

The efficiency claims are supported only by primitive counts. There are no measurements of inference time, rendering speed, peak memory, model parameters, or quality-versus-resource tradeoffs, despite repeated claims of generation 'in seconds' and improved computational efficiency.

Reproducibility is poor even with the supplement: optimizer, learning rates, schedule, training duration, batch composition, dataset subset sizes, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, and sufficient details or code for the customized differentiable rasterizer are absent. Training also requires a 140 GB GPU, with no accessible-resource configuration reported.

Evaluation breadth is narrow for the strength of the claims: rendering is tested on only two benchmarks, the ablation is confined to DL3DV, and there is no controlled comparison at matched primitive counts. In particular, the pixel-aligned baselines use different counts from the detector, so the experiment does not fully separate off-grid placement from representation budget.

Overall, the paper contains a worthwhile decoder idea and encouraging compression-quality results, but the target-image-dependent evaluation, overextended geometry claims, inconsistent technical specification, and incomplete reproducibility currently outweigh the contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and useful alternative to pixel- and voxel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS. Differentiable sub-pixel center prediction, multi-density decoding, and confidence-based multi-view fusion form a technically plausible end-to-end system rather than an isolated heuristic.

The empirical results are strong on DL3DV: the method generally achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across 3–12 input views while using substantially fewer Gaussians. For example, with three views it uses 115.2K Gaussians versus 314.8K for AnySplat and improves PSNR from 17.64 to 20.12.

The controlled ablations support the main design choices. The complete detector improves over similarly sized and substantially denser pixel-aligned variants, while removing adaptive density or confidence causes clear degradation. The confidence ablation is particularly persuasive.

Camera-pose results consistently improve over the pretrained VGGT backbone on Charge, while AnySplat degrades it. This provides interesting evidence that rendering supervision can improve parts of a pretrained reconstruction backbone without additional 3D annotations.

The manuscript is clear and visually effective. The architecture, qualitative artifacts of grid-aligned alternatives, and allocation of confidence across views are explained well, and the limitations concerning unseen regions are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The broad claim that fine-tuning improves geometry is only partially supported. Camera-pose accuracy improves, but every reported Charge depth setting is worse than the original VGGT in both AbsRel and delta<1.25. The DL3DV depth evidence is qualitative because ground-truth depth is unavailable, so the conclusion should distinguish pose improvement from depth performance.

The efficiency evidence is limited to primitive counts. The paper does not report inference latency, rendering speed, peak memory, model size, or training cost, despite emphasizing scalability, generation in seconds, and computational efficiency. The stated requirement of a 140 GB GPU also raises an important practical concern.

Reproducibility is presently weak: optimizer settings, learning rates and schedules, number of iterations, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, exact training-subset sizes, and other consequential details are absent. Two apparent specification errors add ambiguity: the density proportions are stated as 55% + 35% + 15% = 105%, and the opacity regularizer sin(alpha*c) on alpha*c in [0,1] would favor zero rather than both zero and one unless a missing factor such as pi is intended.

The evaluation covers only two test benchmarks and lacks uncertainty estimates. Performance on Charge is mixed: DepthSplat is substantially better in PSNR for the 3-, 6-, and 9-view settings, and AnySplat has better LPIPS in the 25-view setting. Thus, “state-of-the-art” should be qualified by dataset, metric, and view regime.

Novel-view evaluation requires a second forward pass containing the target images to recover their camera poses, with method-specific alignment procedures differing across baselines. Although this follows the closest prior work and does not directly add target primitives to the reconstructed model, it makes the protocol less clean than evaluation with independently supplied target poses and warrants a more explicit discussion of information access and alignment sensitivity.

The adaptive allocation is driven by fixed image-entropy percentiles rather than learned task-specific density selection, while centers remain constrained to image patches and backbone-predicted surfaces. These restrictions do not invalidate the contribution, but they make some claims about fully adaptive primitive placement stronger than the implemented mechanism supports.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned primitive placement. Using differentiable heatmaps and DSNT to obtain continuous patch-local coordinates is technically sensible and produces a compact representation.

The empirical results are strong and broad. Across six held-out datasets, the method reports 21.21 average PSNR versus 18.83 for DA3GS and 17.71 for AnySplat, while using only 0.143 Gaussians per input pixel versus 1.0 and 0.814, respectively.

The controlled placement ablation supports the central contribution: under the authors' pipeline, off-grid placement improves average PSNR from 18.33 to 18.63 and LPIPS from 0.4341 to 0.3796 relative to pixel alignment, and also outperforms direct 3D-offset prediction.

The paper evaluates both appearance and geometry. The depth, pose, and field-of-view results indicate that photometric fine-tuning improves the VGGT backbone rather than merely hiding geometric errors through appearance parameters.

The qualitative results consistently show sharper detail and cleaner extrapolated geometry, and the discussion candidly identifies limitations involving unseen surfaces, view-dependent appearance, and humans.
weaknesses: A material technical inconsistency appears in the opacity regularizer. The paper states that minimizing L_op = sum sin(alpha*c), with alpha*c in [0,1], pushes opacity toward either 0 or 1. Over that interval sin(x) is monotonic, so minimization pushes values only toward 0. If a factor such as pi was omitted, that omission is consequential for correctness and reproducibility.

The pose-free evaluation uses each held-out target image in a second VGGT pass over the context and target images to recover the target camera. Although the target is not used to construct the reported Gaussian model and this follows AnySplat's protocol, it is still target-image access and does not measure synthesis at a novel query pose available without its corresponding image. The headline novel-view-synthesis claim should therefore be interpreted narrowly.

The overall gains cannot be attributed cleanly to off-grid detection. The full model also changes confidence pruning, opacity regularization, geometry losses, and backbone fine-tuning. Table 3 helps isolate placement but covers only two datasets, while the much larger Table 1 gains are against only two systems with different decoders and training procedures.

The adaptive-density component is a fixed entropy heuristic with fixed 55/35/15 percentile allocations rather than a learned allocation policy. The paper provides no comparisons to random, gradient-, feature-, or reconstruction-error-based allocations, so the evidence does not establish that Shannon entropy is the relevant design choice.

The claimed efficiency is supported only by Gaussian count. There are no measurements of inference latency, rendering speed, peak memory, or model FLOPs, despite the use of a 1B-parameter backbone and 140 GB of training memory. Thus, claims such as scene generation 'in seconds' and improved computational efficiency are insufficiently quantified.

Reproducibility is substantially limited: the manuscript omits optimizer settings, learning-rate schedule, training duration, loss weights, Gaussian scale bounds, dataset subset sizes and exact splits, and important rasterizer details. The supplementary implementation section does not supply these items, and the opacity-loss ambiguity compounds the problem.

The experiments report no multiple-run variation or statistical uncertainty, and results averaged across 3, 6, 9, and 12 inputs conceal performance as a function of view count. These omissions make robustness, especially in the sparse-view regime emphasized by the paper, difficult to assess.

strengths: The central idea is relevant and reasonably original: differentiable sub-pixel primitive placement via patch-wise heatmaps is a meaningful alternative to fixed pixel- and voxel-aligned decoding.

The reported novel-view results are strong and consistent across six varied datasets. Table 1 shows large gains over AnySplat and DA3-Giant on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS while reporting only 0.143 Gaussians per input pixel.

The paper includes useful comparisons against pixel-aligned placement and learned 3D offsets, as well as ablations of adaptive density and confidence pruning. The qualitative examples generally support the claimed improvements in sharpness and artifact reduction.

The method combines a strong reconstruction backbone with a comparatively simple decoder, requires no 3D annotations during its fine-tuning stage, and acknowledges relevant limitations such as unseen regions, view-dependent appearance, and poor handling of humans.

The manuscript is visually clear, and its architecture and high-level training pipeline are easy to follow. weaknesses: The main evaluation does not cleanly isolate rendering quality. Target images are included in a second N+T-image forward pass to estimate target cameras, so the headline NVS metrics depend on target-image-assisted localization and conflate camera estimation with representation quality. Results using ground-truth target cameras after a fixed context-only alignment, or a clearly standardized identical alignment for every baseline, are needed to substantiate the broad state-of-the-art rendering claim.

The comparison set is narrow: only AnySplat and DA3-Giant appear in the principal table, despite the paper discussing several pose-free feed-forward methods. The manuscript does not provide quantitative comparisons to FLARE, PF3Splat, NoPoSplat, Splatt3R, SPFSplat, or SelfSplat, nor explain in sufficient detail why none can be evaluated. This weakens the state-of-the-art claim.

The efficiency/scalability claims are supported only by Gaussian count. There are no measurements of inference time, rendering FPS, peak memory, model size, or training cost beyond requiring a 140-GB GPU. Moreover, all evaluation images are capped at 518 pixels, so the claimed opportunity to process high-resolution images is not demonstrated.

Important method specifications are internally inconsistent. The density proportions are stated as 55%, 35%, and 15%, which sum to 105%. The opacity regularizer is written as sin(alpha*c); on alpha*c in [0,1], minimizing this expression favors zero rather than both binary endpoints as claimed, unless a factor such as pi is missing. Equation 1 also sums spatial heatmap coordinates to P even though P was defined as the number of primitive channels. These ambiguities prevent assessing or reproducing the exact implemented method.

Reproducibility is inadequate even with the supplementary pages: the complete weighted objective is never given, and loss weights, scale bounds, optimizer, learning rate and schedule, training duration, dataset subset sizes and sampling ratios, and several architectural details are absent. The project-page field is blank and no code availability is stated.

The ablations do not fully establish the proposed causal story. Table 3 does not report or match primitive budgets across placement variants, while Table 4 lacks a neither-adaptive-nor-confidence condition, primitive counts, and controls against other allocation heuristics. Thus the individual benefit of entropy allocation versus changed capacity or regularization remains uncertain.

The use of a supervised, large-scale pretrained VGGT teacher is reasonable, but descriptions such as training "from images only" and "self-supervised" should be qualified: the approach inherits substantial supervised geometric knowledge and explicitly regularizes toward VGGT pseudo-targets. This is primarily a clarity issue, unlike the evaluation and reproducibility concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: tying primitive locations and counts to a regular pixel or voxel grid. The proposed differentiable, sub-pixel placement based on patch-level heatmaps is intuitive, technically plausible, and meaningfully adapted to this setting.

The empirical gains are substantial and consistent across six held-out benchmarks. Averaged over the reported datasets, the method obtains 21.21 PSNR, 0.6470 SSIM, and 0.3532 LPIPS, compared with 18.83/0.5428/0.3834 for DA3-GS and 17.71/0.5075/0.3937 for AnySplat.

The quality improvements are achieved with a compact representation: the reported primitive-to-input-pixel ratio is 0.143, versus 0.814 for AnySplat and 1.0 for DA3-GS. This is a practically useful result, even though end-to-end efficiency measurements are missing.

The ablations support the main components. Off-grid placement improves the two-dataset average over the pixel-aligned variant from 18.33 to 18.63 PSNR and reduces LPIPS from 0.4341 to 0.3796. Adaptive density and confidence pruning also produce sizable improvements on DL3DV, especially in LPIPS.

The geometry evaluation adds useful evidence beyond image-rendering metrics. Fine-tuning improves the VGGT backbone's reported average depth, pose, and field-of-view errors, while the qualitative results show cleaner geometry and fewer grid or floating artifacts.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective. The architecture, training loop, qualitative comparisons, and stated limitations—unobserved regions, view-dependent appearance, and weak performance on humans—are easy to understand.
weaknesses: The efficiency claims are supported only by primitive counts. The paper repeatedly emphasizes reconstruction 'in seconds,' scalability, and computational efficiency, but reports no reconstruction latency, rendering FPS, peak memory, model size, or comparison under matched hardware. This materially limits the practical claim.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript omits the complete loss equation and loss weights, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, number of iterations, training duration, exact dataset subset sizes, sampling proportions, and several Gaussian scale bounds. The supplementary material supplies only partial architectural details, and the project-page entry is blank.

There are technical inconsistencies in the specification. The adaptive-density proportions are stated as 55%, 35%, and 15%, which sum to 105%. Moreover, the proposed opacity regularizer is written as sum sin(alpha*c); on alpha*c in [0,1], this is minimized at zero rather than at both zero and one, contradicting the stated goal of encouraging binary opacity. These points require clarification to establish the exact implemented method.

The primitive-placement ablation does not cleanly isolate off-grid positioning. The pixel-aligned baseline predicts one Gaussian per pixel and therefore differs greatly in primitive count and decoding structure. A grid-aligned baseline with the same per-patch primitive budget would better establish that continuous placement, rather than sparsity or decoder design, causes the gain.

The comparison is limited to two recent systems despite a broader related-work discussion and a state-of-the-art claim. The manuscript does not quantitatively compare with other pose-free feed-forward methods or explain in sufficient detail why such comparisons are infeasible. Results are also averaged across input-view counts, obscuring performance as the number of views changes.

The evaluation protocol uses a second forward pass containing both context and target images to obtain target camera poses. Although the rendered Gaussian model comes from context images and the protocol follows AnySplat, target RGB is still consumed by the pose estimator. The paper should more clearly delimit this transductive setting and ensure every baseline uses exactly the same protocol.

Exact evaluation scene counts and split identities are not fully documented, and DL3DV appears in both the training-data list and evaluation. The assertion that evaluation sets are held out is reassuring but insufficient for checking scene-level disjointness or possible overlap with VGGT pretraining.

The fixed entropy-based density assignment is only moderately novel and receives limited analysis. There is no comparison with learned density selection, gradient-based detail measures, alternative thresholds, or a primitive-count/quality curve. Consequently, the specific value of the proposed 16/32/64 allocation remains under-supported.

No variability, confidence intervals, or repeated-run results are reported. This is less concerning for the large headline gains, but it weakens interpretation of the smaller placement and geometry improvements. Overall, the strong and broad empirical results support a weak accept, while the technical specification and efficiency evidence prevent a higher rating.
